notes: Permission to appeal on s30(1)(f) redevelopment ground; conservation area consent timing and perjury argument rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Platia v Thermatic: section 30(1)(f) refusal and conservation area consent timing
key_facts: Mr Platia sought a new tenancy of 34 Broadway Market E8 but the recorder refused renewal under section 30(1)(f) because Thermatic intended substantial redevelopment works requiring possession.
Planning permission existed but conservation area consent for the Hackney conservation area was outstanding at the hearing on 7 June 2004.
Post-hearing letters from Hackney suggested the conservation application had not been validly made at the hearing, though consent was granted on 26 October 2004.
The tenant did not attend below; on permission to appeal Neuberger LJ refused the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against refusal of a new business tenancy under section 30(1)(f) of the 1954 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the recorder was entitled to find redevelopment intention and conservation consent would be obtained within a reasonable time.
enrichment.ratio: Section 30(1)(f) does not require a landlord to be ready to commence works the instant the tenancy expires; a reasonable expectation that conservation area consent will follow shortly after expiry suffices, and fresh post-hearing evidence did not establish perjury on the central issue.
legal_issues: Whether absence of conservation area consent at tenancy expiry defeated the section 30(1)(f) ground
Whether the recorder was misled by evidence that consent was merely held up in administration
Whether perjured evidence vitiated the refusal of a new tenancy

notes: Employment remedies appeal; ET quantified loss by loan interest rather than conventional salary mitigation analysis.

enrichment.short_title: AON Training v Dore: remittal of compensatory award based on business-loan interest
key_facts: Mr Dore, a dyslexic employee, was unfairly dismissed and unlawfully discriminated against by AON Training Ltd and its controlling director Mr O'Neill.

At the remedies hearing the employment tribunal awarded compensatory sums including interest on £48,122.82 borrowed to start a refurbishing business, rather than assessing lost salary net of business earnings.
The EAT largely upheld the awards but the Court of Appeal granted permission on whether loan-interest awards were a proper head of compensatory loss.
Peter Gibson LJ inferred the tribunal thought self-employment mitigation was reasonable but its reasoning on quantum was inadequate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal limited to remedies after liability findings in employment tribunal and EAT proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; disputed compensatory and interest elements set aside and remitted to a fresh employment tribunal, with conditional costs order.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employee mitigates by starting a business, the conventional approach under both ERA and DDA is to assess lost remuneration, add reasonable mitigation costs and deduct earnings from the new venture; awarding interest on borrowings without identifying the loss mitigated or explaining the calculation is not a sustainable compensatory award.
legal_issues: Whether interest on a business loan is recoverable as compensatory loss for unfair dismissal
Whether the same tort-based quantification principles apply under the DDA
Whether inadequate tribunal reasons required remittal rather than substitution
linked_authorities: Gardiner-Hill v Roland Berger Technics Ltd [1982] IRLR 498
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 2409

notes: Colman J upheld permanent anti-suit injunction; subrogated insurers bound to London arbitration on tort subrogation claim.

enrichment.short_title: West Tankers: anti-suit injunction and subrogated insurers bound by charterparty arbitration

statutes_considered.title: New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards 1958

key_facts: After collision damage at an Erg refinery in Syracuse, subrogated Italian insurers pursued Owners of the Front Comor in the Tribunale di Syracuse while Erg's uninsured claim proceeded in London arbitration under the Asbatankvoy charterparty.
Gross J granted an interim anti-suit injunction against the insurers, who were not present at that hearing.
The insurers applied to discharge the injunction, arguing Turner v Grovit, Italian law of subrogation and that they were not bound by the English-law arbitration clause.
Colman J held English law governed whether the duty to arbitrate transferred with the subrogated tort claim and confirmed a permanent injunction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside an interim anti-suit injunction restraining Italian court proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permanent injunction substituted and insurers held bound to arbitrate the subrogated delict claim in London.
enrichment.ratio: Under English conflicts rules the subject-matter of subrogation to a tort claim enforceable only by an English-law arbitration agreement includes the inseparable duty to arbitrate; pursuing foreign court proceedings inconsistently with that agreement warrants anti-suit relief notwithstanding Article II.3 and foreign courts' attitude to such orders.
legal_issues: Which law governs transfer by subrogation of the duty to arbitrate
Effect of Italian Civil Code Article 1916 subrogation on arbitration obligations
Whether Turner v Grovit precludes anti-suit injunctions supporting arbitration agreements
Whether absence of actionable breach of contract defeats Angelic Grace relief

notes: Service-out order set aside; Ghanaian company failed forum conveniens and merits threshold on trust tracing claim against Jersey trustee.

enrichment.short_title: NABB Brothers v Lloyds Offshore: service out set aside in Guernsey trust tracing claim
key_facts: NABB Brothers Ltd, a Ghanaian company, claimed a former managing director misappropriated business funds through Lloyds Bank London accounts into the Tubuoh Trust administered by a Guernsey/Jersey trustee.

Master Bowman granted service out under CPR 6.20 on constructive trust and restitution grounds; only about £700,000 transferred in May 1994 remained viable after disclosure showed fixed-deposit statements did not relate to the trust account.
The defendant migrated to Jersey and argued material non-disclosure, weak merits and that Guernsey was the proper forum for trust administration.
Lawrence Collins J set aside the service-out order primarily for want of forum conveniens.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Challenge to an without-notice order permitting service out of the jurisdiction on a foreign trustee.
enrichment.outcome: Service-out order set aside; England not the proper place to bring the claim despite arguable constructive trust and territorial-link points.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a foreign trustee receives funds transferred from London bank accounts, the natural forum for a dispute about administration of a Guernsey-law discretionary trust and Beddoe directions is Guernsey/Jersey, and a claimant must clearly show England is the appropriate forum under CPR 6.21(2A).
legal_issues: Whether CPR 6.20(14) and (15) were satisfied by London transfer instructions
Whether a proprietary equitable claim falls within restitution for service-out purposes
Forum conveniens between England, Ghana and Guernsey/Jersey
Merits threshold on knowing receipt and tracing against an innocent volunteer trustee

notes: Fatal police shooting; Wilding/Hoddinott reports withheld; assault and misfeasance claims struck out after negligence admissions.

enrichment.short_title: Ashley v Sussex Police: strike-out after fatal armed raid and admitted negligence
key_facts: James Ashley was fatally shot by PC Sherwood during an early-hours drugs raid at Hastings in January 1998 after intelligence portrayed him as a dangerous armed offender.
Criminal prosecutions of officers failed or were withdrawn; Sussex Police admitted negligence causing death and negligent release of the deceased's name before informing the family.
Claimants sought disclosure of ACC Wilding and Sir John Hoddinott inquiry reports and pursued assault and misfeasance in public office claims alongside admitted negligence.
Dobbs J refused report disclosure on relevance/PII, struck out assault and misfeasance claims and entered summary judgment for the police on those heads.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications for disclosure and strike-out/summary judgment in a civil claim arising from a fatal police shooting.
enrichment.outcome: Inquiry reports not disclosed; assault claim and both pre- and post-shooting misfeasance claims struck out or summarily dismissed; negligence damages to proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where police admit liability for death and consequential injury, an assault claim based on self-defence has no real prospect of success; misfeasance requires deliberate bad faith or reckless indifference to legality, not merely serious negligence or corporate failure, and opinion investigation reports are normally irrelevant to civil trial.
legal_issues: Public interest immunity over police complaint investigation reports
Whether unlawful force assault survives admitted negligence causing death
Ingredients of misfeasance in public office after Three Rivers (No 3)
Whether exemplary damages could justify continuing misfeasance litigation

notes: Section 25 GL(GP) Act appeal; interruption of short-term lettings reset enforcement immunity for temporary sleeping use.

enrichment.short_title: Fairstate v SoS: section 25 and loss of immunity after break in short-term lettings
key_facts: Westminster enforcement notice alleged Flat 3 Marylebone High Street changed from permanent residential use to temporary sleeping accommodation under section 25 without planning permission.
Fairstate had operated short-term lettings for over ten years to January 1999, then Miss Kapoor occupied for 155 consecutive days before short lets resumed in July 1999.
An inspector upheld the notice; Sullivan J dismissed the appeal holding section 25 deemed a fresh material change when short-term use resumed.
The Court of Appeal restored Westminster's control policy over short-term residential use in central London.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from dismissal of a planning appeal against an enforcement notice on ten-year immunity grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; resumption of section 25 use after a significant break was a fresh material change not protected by earlier immunity.
enrichment.ratio: Section 25 is a deeming provision that treats any change to temporary sleeping accommodation in Greater London as a material change of use; lawful status acquired by ten years' short-term use can be lost when continuity is broken by longer residential occupation and short-term use later resumes.
legal_issues: Whether a non-material intermediate use preserves ten-year immunity for section 25 use
Construction and purpose of section 25 in London planning control
Interaction between section 191(2) immunity and section 25 deeming

notes: Landlord and Tenant Act 1988 consent appeal allowed; Telco covenant concerns made refusal of underletting reasonable.

enrichment.short_title: NCR v Riverland: reasonable refusal of consent to underletting with reverse premium
key_facts: NCR sought Riverland's consent to underlet Solar House Finchley to Telco Global Ltd with a £3 million reverse premium because open-market rent was below the headlease rent of £710,000.
Peter Smith J held Riverland breached the 1988 Act by delaying and unreasonably refusing consent, focusing on NCR's continuing head-tenant covenant.
Riverland refused on financial terms and Telco's weak covenant; expert evidence valued the reversion about £500,000 lower with a Telco underlease because of 1954 Act renewal rights.
The Court of Appeal held about three weeks was a reasonable decision time and Telco's covenant concerns were a reasonable ground for refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against declarations that a landlord unreasonably delayed and unreasonably withheld consent to an underletting.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declarations set aside and refusal of consent held reasonable in time and substance.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 1988 Act a landlord need only show that some reasonable landlords might refuse consent for the stated reasons; concern about a weak undertenant's effect on reversion value after expiry of a strong head lease can be reasonable even where the head tenant remains primarily liable.
legal_issues: What period is reasonable to decide a consent application under section 1(3)
Whether undertenant covenant strength is irrelevant given head-tenant liability
Effect of a reverse premium on compliance with best-rent underletting covenants
Measure of damages for breach of statutory duty under section 4

notes: Moore-Bick J appointed arbitrator under s18; Finnish statutory insurer claimant treated as party to Club arbitration.

enrichment.short_title: Through Transport v New India: section 18 appointment where statutory insurer must arbitrate
key_facts: New India, having settled a cargo loss, pursued the P&I Club in Finland under section 67 of the Finnish Insurance Contracts Act after Borneo Maritime Oy was struck off.
The Court of Appeal declared New India bound to arbitrate in London under the Club Rules but discharged Moore-Bick J's anti-suit injunction.
The Club applied under section 18 for appointment of an arbitrator to obtain a non-liability award before any Finnish merits judgment.
New India argued it was not a party to an arbitration agreement and the court lacked jurisdiction to appoint.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 18 of the 1996 Act to appoint an arbitrator after a jurisdictional declaration and partial anti-suit relief.
enrichment.outcome: Arbitrator appointed; New India treated as claiming under the insured member and bound by the Club's London arbitration clause once it sought indemnity.
enrichment.ratio: A statutory third-party claimant enforcing an English insurance obligation acquires a chose in action subject to the contract's arbitration clause; once it makes a demand on the insurer a dispute arises that either party may refer to arbitration, enabling section 18 appointment even without a contractual novation.
legal_issues: Whether section 18 jurisdiction requires a full arbitration agreement between applicant and respondent
Characterisation of Finnish statutory direct-action rights under English conflicts rules
Discretion to appoint an arbitrator to obtain a defensive award against foreign proceedings
Distinction between breach of contract and obligation to arbitrate after Through Transport

notes: Unusual costs orders in contact proceedings; mother ordered to pay after unreasonable obstruction and sexual-abuse allegations.

enrichment.short_title: Re T (a child): costs against resident parent for unreasonable contact litigation
key_facts: Protracted contact dispute over child J ended with residence transferred to the father after fact-finding hearings before HH Judge Kushner QC.
The mother repeatedly frustrated contact, resiled from agreements and raised unfounded sexual-abuse allegations despite clear findings that contact was in J's interests.
The father limited his costs claim to three hearings where false or unnecessary litigation occurred, totalling about £20,000.
The Court of Appeal upheld exceptional costs orders against the mother while praising the judge's case management.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against costs orders made in private law children proceedings after residence and contact litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; costs orders for December 2002 and May/August 2003 hearings upheld and referred for detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Costs in children cases are exceptional but may be ordered where a resident parent's conduct of the litigation is unreasonable, including persisting with fact-finding and abuse allegations after objective findings that contact should proceed; personality-driven distortion does not excuse obstruction once the court has resolved the welfare facts.
legal_issues: When costs may be ordered between parents in children proceedings
Distinction between unreasonable litigation conduct and disputed welfare decisions
Effect of expert findings rejecting sexual-abuse allegations on costs
Whether costs orders deter legitimate contact disputes

notes: Section 67 challenge failed; CL(C)A 1978 contribution claim for PDS breaches held outside Implementation Contract arbitration clause.

enrichment.short_title: X Ltd v Y Ltd: section 67 confirms no arbitration jurisdiction over PDS contribution claim
key_facts: Corrosion in a specialised plant led to separate PDS and Implementation contracts between A and Y; X later replaced A as employer under the Implementation Contract only.
After further corrosion and a settlement with A, X pursued arbitration against Y for contribution relating to PDS breaches, Implementation breaches and pre-contract misrepresentations.
The tribunal held it had jurisdiction over the misrepresentation claim but not over a section 1 contribution claim founded on PDS Contract breaches.
Jackson J on a section 67 rehearing confirmed the interim award, treating the contracts as separate with distinct arbitration clauses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 67 challenge to an arbitral tribunal's interim jurisdictional award under Part 8 procedure in the TCC.
enrichment.outcome: Interim award confirmed; Claim 1 for contribution based on PDS breaches falls outside the Implementation Contract arbitration clause.
enrichment.ratio: A contribution claim under the 1978 Act for breaches of an earlier PDS contract is not a dispute 'relating to' a later implementation contract merely because both concerned the same plant; separate contracts with mirror arbitration clauses keep PDS claims within the PDS arbitration agreement unless rights were transferred.
legal_issues: Construction of 'disputes... relating to the Contract' in a standard ICC-style arbitration clause
Whether a section 1 contribution claim can be shoehorned into the later contract's arbitration agreement
Effect of employer substitution under clause 23 on arbitration scope
Section 67 standard of full rehearing on jurisdiction
